Disha had never met Bidisha. She noted the name. During: Two weeks later, in the lift, someone joked, "If Bidisha's on your project, you'll sleep well." Disha smiled; she already believed it. After: The next month, Disha was paired with Bidisha on a campaign. On the first day, Bidisha sent a clear plan by ten, answered every question within the hour, and flagged a mistake before it cost them. Disha thought: I knew all this before she did a thing for me. It had been built by a hundred small things for other people.

qa.q: How late did Bidisha once stay to fix a designer's file?
qa.a: Till midnight.

qa.q: What does Disha's final thought suggest about how she felt?
qa.a: It suggests she felt impressed and thoughtful, realising Bidisha's reputation had reached her long before they worked together.

qa.q: What could Disha learn from Bidisha for her own reputation?
qa.a: That consistent small actions, like clear plans and quick answers, get noticed and passed on.

qa.q: How might Bidisha feel if she knew what people said about her?
qa.a: She would likely feel pleased and valued, seeing her reliability recognised.

grounding: Shows a young professional hearing about a colleague's reliability before meeting her, and seeing how reputation is passed on.

subtype: Reputation travels through others [Observer]
passage: Nitin, beta, you asked me how people in this office decide who to trust. Let me tell you what I learnt at your age, when I, Madhuri, was a young woman of twenty-four and new at the bank. In my first month, I heard two officers talking about a clerk called Pillai. "If Pillai says the cash tallies, it tallies." Another said, "Don't give Mehta your files, they come back late and messy." I'd met neither of them. But when I needed help with a difficult ledger, whom did I go to? Pillai. He'd never met me either. His good name had walked ahead of him. From then on I tried to be someone people would talk about like that. Small things, done right, every single day.

qa.q: What was said about Pillai?
qa.a: "If Pillai says the cash tallies, it tallies."

qa.q: How did young Madhuri feel after hearing about Pillai and Mehta?
qa.a: She felt curious and a bit wary, forming views of people she had never met.

qa.q: What choice in the story came from what Madhuri heard?
qa.a: She went to Pillai for help with a difficult ledger, and then decided to build that kind of reputation herself.

qa.q: How might Mehta be affected by the officers' talk?
qa.a: Mehta might lose chances and trust from newcomers before they ever see his work.

grounding: Illustrates an elder recalling, as a young professional, how reputations travelled before she met people.

subtype: Repairing broken trust [Response]
passage: In Berlin, Bilal and Freya had shared a small translation business for a year. In March, Bilal missed a deadline for their biggest client because he'd taken on too much and didn't tell her. Freya found out when the client called, furious. Bilal didn't make excuses. "I let you down. I should have told you a week ago." He worked the whole weekend to fix it, and gave up his share of the fee. Freya accepted it coolly. For months, she checked his work. He didn't complain. He sent drafts early, flagged problems the moment he saw them, and never missed another date. In October, Freya passed him a big project without checking. "You've got this," she said. Bilal didn't say anything. He just nodded.

qa.q: When did Bilal miss the deadline?
qa.a: In March.

qa.q: How did Bilal likely feel when Freya kept checking his work for months?
qa.a: He probably felt uncomfortable but patient and determined, accepting that he had to earn back her trust.

qa.q: What did Bilal do to repair the trust?
qa.a: He admitted it plainly, worked the weekend to fix it, gave up his share of the fee, and then stayed reliable for months without demanding forgiveness.

qa.q: How does Freya's trust change over the year?
qa.a: Freya goes from cool and watchful to confident enough, by October, to pass him a big project without checking.

grounding: Shows a young adult who let a partner down admitting it, making amends and slowly regaining trust through reliability.

subtype: Repairing broken trust [Response]
passage: In the school staff room, Elizabeth had forgotten to submit Deepika's class marks to the office, and the report cards went out with blanks. Parents complained to Deepika, who hadn't known. The next morning, Elizabeth went straight to her. "It was my fault. I forgot. I've told the principal, and I'll call every parent myself today." She did, one by one, through lunch. Deepika said only, "Okay." For the rest of the term, Elizabeth submitted everything two days early and copied Deepika in. She never asked, "Are we fine now?" In the last week, Deepika left a sticky note on her desk: "Can you check my marks sheet before I send it? I trust you with it."

qa.q: What went out with blanks?
qa.a: The report cards.

qa.q: How might Deepika have felt when parents complained?
qa.a: She likely felt embarrassed and angry, blamed for something she didn't know about.

qa.q: Which of Elizabeth's actions helped rebuild trust most?
qa.a: Calling every parent herself, then submitting early all term without asking to be forgiven.

qa.q: How does Deepika's sticky note show her view has changed?
qa.a: It shows Deepika now trusts Elizabeth again, after seeing reliable work over a whole term.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult who admits a mistake, makes amends and rebuilds trust slowly through consistent reliability.

subtype: Repairing broken trust [Response]
passage:
Dear Lalremsiami,
I know you don't owe me a reply. I told Mira about your family trouble after you trusted me with it. I told myself I was asking for advice, but that's not true. I was careless with something that wasn't mine. I'm sorry. I've already told Mira that I shouldn't have shared it and asked her to keep it to herself. I'm not writing to ask you to forgive me or to be friends again right away. I understand if you need time, or if you don't want that. I'll keep doing what I should have done before: keeping your confidences and turning up when I say I will. If you ever want to talk, I'll be here. If not, I'll respect that.
Harsha

qa.q: Who did Harsha tell about Lalremsiami's family trouble?
qa.a: Mira.

qa.q: How does Harsha seem to feel while writing this letter?
qa.a: Harsha feels ashamed and regretful for breaking the confidence, but determined not to pressure Lalremsiami.

qa.q: What makes this apology a good start at repairing trust?
qa.a: Harsha admits it plainly, has already made amends with Mira, promises reliability, and does not demand quick forgiveness.

qa.q: How might Lalremsiami feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Lalremsiami may still feel hurt and wary, but perhaps a little respected by the honesty and the space given.

grounding: Shows a young adult admitting a breach of trust, making amends and not demanding quick forgiveness.
